---
title: "The number of ordered grade reports"
subtitle: "2.3 · after the postrank theory book, ch. 14, and the postrank vignette m5"
description: "Sizes of unrestricted, grade-restricted and fixed-order report families."
---

An ordered grade report groups the units and specifies the order of the groups. Thus, the full family contains every strict ranking and every report that gives some units the same grade. A cap on the number of occupied grades reduces this family. A fixed-order family contains only reports formed by cutting that order. The curves compare the sizes of these families on a logarithmic scale. The small examples show which changes to the grouping or order produce a distinct report.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Three units.** There are 13 ordered grade reports but only 6 strict rankings. In the small examples,
  some reports group letters, while others give each letter its own box. Swapping the positions of occupied boxes
  changes which directions are stated.
- **Six units.** There are 4,683 reports in all. The cap permits 603, the exact grade count permits 540, and cuts of one declared order permit 32. The capped family includes reports with fewer occupied grades, which explains
  its larger count than the exact family.
- **Eight units.** All reports reach 545,835, compared with 6,051 under the cap and 128 along one order. Colors and dash patterns identify the families even when their counts are close. The legend shows counts at the selected number of units, and the labels at the right show counts for twelve units. The arrow-key reader and table give every count.
- **Twelve units.** There are 28,091,567,595 reports in the full family, while the cap leaves 523,251. The hollow
  squares mark problem sizes encountered elsewhere in this collection. Counting those possibilities does not
  require generating every report.
- **An empty exact family.** The small example has 0 reports: the requested number of nonempty grades exceeds
  its number of units. An empty family has no logarithmic height, so its count stays in the table of exact counts.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
A report that follows a declared order can cut only between adjacent units in that order. This example has no equal-score blocks. These counts describe the number of eligible reports. The posterior risks and the work required to find the best report depend on the particular problem and algorithm.
:::

Standalone: [report counts](../../embed/how-many-reports.html), for example `?n=8&G=3`.
